stories.imageAlt: A photo of a smiling bearded man in a blue button-down shirt holding a smiling toddler. The caption reads: “This is my Daddy Travis. We love to play pretend together.”
stories.body:
By Faith Alone

The stories of Evelyn and Marshall Phillips offer a rare view into the Followers of Christ — and reveal both the power and limits of Oregon’s efforts to compel parents to seek medical care for their children.

Co-published with The Oregonian

The deputy medical examiner thought the family was being evasive. Eric Tonsfeldt had been dispatched to the pistachio-green house in Oregon City on the night of March 5, 2017. Inside he found Sarah Mitchell in bed, her dead newborn in her arms.

Mitchell is a member of the Followers of Christ, a sect known for refusing medical treatment. She had received no prenatal care. Three women without medical training guided her delivery that afternoon.

Tonsfeldt listened as the family insisted that the baby, whom they had named Ginnifer, had seemed healthy for most of the afternoon, then suddenly stopped breathing. They couldn’t explain why the baby appeared so underweight. Their answers to many of Tonsfeldt’s questions were vague. Nobody would make eye contact with him.

Later, investigators would discover that 13 minutes after Ginnifer’s birth, Followers began exchanging a series of worried texts. “Not good breathing,” one wrote in a group chat. Another requested prayers: “She’s really bad.” (One person in the chat would later advise deleting the messages.)

No one had called 911 as the gaps between each breath increased. When asked why not, Ginnifer’s father later said, “Because it’s in God’s hands.” He anointed his daughter with olive oil and wept as he prayed that she would be OK. Ginnifer died in his arms at 7 p.m., four hours after she was born.

Tonsfeldt gently collected the newborn and examined her in another room. She weighed 3½ pounds, roughly half that of an average full-term infant. He found no signs of injury or trauma.

The medical examiner still felt that something was awry. To play for time, he asked if someone would make him a cup of coffee and headed to the kitchen. As Tonsfeldt waited, one of the baby’s grandfathers approached him and blurted out an unexpected question: Would it make a difference if Ginnifer had a twin?

There was another baby, a girl named Evelyn. She was alive.

In the dim light of a bathroom, Tonsfeldt found women huddled over a tiny newborn, who was barely making a sound. They were feeding her from an eyedropper.

He told the family to get her to a hospital. After Evelyn’s grandfather made it clear they weren’t going anywhere, Tonsfeldt summoned the police, who delivered an ultimatum: Take Evelyn to the hospital or they’d do it themselves.

Evelyn’s family relented. A patrol car followed to make sure they got there. She was admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit in Portland with respiratory distress syndrome. With the help of a breathing machine and a feeding tube, Evelyn began to stabilize. An autopsy would later conclude the same condition, common in premature babies, had caused her sister’s death.

The Mitchells were charged with murder by neglect, as well as criminal mistreatment for failing to get Evelyn medical care. That left authorities with another challenge: Who would care for Evelyn?

Her family assumed any custody arrangement would be temporary and suggested Marshall and Jennifer Phillips, a couple born and raised in the Followers. But Marshall was no ordinary Follower. Once, when his young son became gravely ill, he brought him to a hospital. In the eyes of the state, that made Marshall and his wife suitable candidates to look after Evelyn.

Evelyn’s family didn’t know then that Marshall’s choice to save his son had set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known. And that he would take Evelyn with him.

For more than a century, states have wrestled with how to address the deaths of children whose parents refuse them medical care for religious reasons. As early as 1901, a father in New York who believed in the “power of God to heal the sick through prayer” was prosecuted for failing to call a doctor for his young daughter who died from pneumonia. Since then, courts have repeatedly held — in cases where Christian Scientists refused treatment or Jehovah’s Witnesses declined blood transfusions — that adults are free to reject medical care for themselves.

Whether they can be compelled to provide medical care for their children is another matter, one that’s been left to states to decide. Courts have generally deferred to legislatures on this question.

Video: This Secretive Religious Sect Doesn’t Believe in Medical Care

Marshall Phillips was raised in the Followers of Christ, which forbids medical care. When his son fell gravely ill, he took him to the hospital. That choice set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known.

For decades, Oregon’s law gave latitude to faith healing and authorities did little to intervene. Between 1989 and 1999, 18 children of the Oregon City-based Followers died. (The sect numbered between 1,500 and 2,000 at its peak.) Most or all of those deaths were preventable, according to the state medical examiner at the time, who estimated that the child death rate in the sect was 26 times that of the general population.

The revelation of those deaths, in The Oregonian and other news outlets, prompted state lawmakers to act. In 1999, they removed spiritual treatment as a defense for second-degree manslaughter and criminal mistreatment. In 2008, prosecutors filed their first case against Followers parents after a 15-month-old died from untreated bronchial pneumonia and a blood infection. A jury convicted the girl’s father of a single count of criminal mistreatment, a misdemeanor, and acquitted her mother.

Two more children in the sect died without medical attention during this period, prompting the Legislature in 2011 to do away with the spiritual defense for any crime. Among those supporting the change: the Christian Science church, which by then had softened its stance amid a steep decline in membership. In a letter to lawmakers that year, a church official wrote: “Spiritual care should never be practiced at the expense of a child’s life.”

Changes in Oregon law — and prosecutors’ willingness to pursue parents who watched their children die — spurred a slow but perceptible shift: Deaths of children in the Followers have become an anomaly. Ginnifer Mitchell’s death in 2017 came amid that yearslong decline. Since then, one child has died due to lack of medical care.

During this same time frame in Idaho, where the laws protect parents who rely only on faith healing, reporting by ProPublica found at least 11 babies and children of Followers died from treatable conditions.

Still, Ginnifer’s death shows how the most entrenched elements of faith-healing communities resist aggressive enforcement. Sarah Mitchell chose to give birth without doctors or nurses, even as her sister was in prison for failing to provide medical care for her premature newborn, who died in 2009. And Sarah’s lack of prenatal care was such that she realized she was carrying twins only when her labor continued after her first baby emerged.

Evelyn might not have survived if police didn’t have the law on their side, allowing them to intervene and demand that her parents take her to the hospital.

The stories of Evelyn and Marshall Phillips — still the subject of legal proceedings today — offer a rare view into the closed community and reveal both the power and the limits of the state’s efforts to compel parents to seek medical care for their children.

Marshall’s ancestors were among the earliest members of the Followers, whose history dates to the late 1800s, when faith-healing sects were active in the Midwest. The faithful later migrated west, starting congregations in Idaho. In the 1930s, a charismatic Followers preacher named Walter White left Idaho for Oregon City, then a lively hub for the timber and paper industries. White’s emotional sermons earned him the moniker “the crying preacher.”

Followers believed the devout earned their place in the afterlife through good acts. They also believed that God heals. The doctrine stems from a passage in the Book of James, which proclaims “And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up.” Seeking medical care was viewed as an abandonment of faith. Those who visited doctors risked being shunned.

By the 1950s, White broke ties with other Followers congregations. He later said that Christ had visited him in a dream and told him the world would soon end and so would baptisms.

White died in 1969 at age 67. Baptisms ended after that, effectively sealing the faithful from the outside world. The Followers never identified White’s successor. To this day, the congregation has no pastor. The lack of a spiritual leader seems only to have intensified members’ influence on one another.

The sect’s practices include other unusual elements: The Bible doesn’t figure in their services, which consist mostly of congregants singing hymns.

In many respects, Followers lead conventional lives. As a boy born in 1975, Marshall rode his bike, ate sugary treats, watched TV and listened to 1980s rock bands like Van Halen. His parents took him and his siblings camping and saved up for trips to Disneyland.

But his life was also circumscribed by his faith. Several times a week, he accompanied his parents to functions at the beige meetinghouse set back from busy Molalla Avenue in Oregon City. Starting at age 7, Followers’ children are separated by gender and age into their own pews. Marshall understood that he would grow up, and grow old, with the kids seated around him. He was instructed not to befriend kids outside the church. Followers considered them “worldly,” the sect’s derisive term for those focused on terrestrial, rather than celestial, concerns.

Like his peers, Marshall never visited a pediatrician. He was never vaccinated. His mom anointed his forehead with extra virgin olive oil when his head throbbed. He endured chicken pox and whooping cough and eventually recovered from both — proof, he believed, of God’s healing powers.

His parents, like others in the sect, made exceptions for dental care. They accepted the use of Novocain but refused the ibuprofen the dentist recommended to address lingering pain after a procedure.

Marshall knew from a young age that his future would be determined by the church. He figured he’d work for a Follower. He’d marry one, too. Marshall and Jennifer went on their first date in a courtship ritual the Followers call a carload — small groups of teens who drive together to get ice cream or coffee. She was 14 and he was 18. They married when Jennifer turned 17, the age girls in the Followers typically wed.

Jennifer’s father had died the year before, surrounded by men from the church. Members were expected to care for the dying, with men tending to men and women to women. Her father never went to the doctor, and family members think he died from heart failure. He was 37.

Women typically give birth in their parents’ homes, and Jennifer was no exception. She delivered her first child, Mary, in the living room, attended by her mother, her mother-in-law, aunts and other women. Marshall was there, too. The rest of the men waited out of sight, smoke from their cigarettes drifting into the living room. She had two more children after that, both sons.

Today, at 50, Marshall looks like the epitome of a suburban dad. With his receding hairline, beard and broad physique, you could picture him browsing the aisles of The Home Depot. He possesses a gentle quality and doesn’t shy away from even harsh self-reflection.

The Followers abide by what they view as traditional gender roles, with men leading their households. Many male Followers work as contractors, electricians and plumbers; Marshall works as a consultant for a heating and air conditioning company. Women mostly focus on the home and their children. Jennifer cleans houses to supplement their income and homeschooled their kids for a time.

As a Follower, Marshall said he pressured his children to fit in at church. He believed the sect’s teachings about earning one’s way to salvation, and he spent many Sunday afternoons visiting the sick and caring for the dying. He and his wife never challenged the institution that shaped their lives.

The couple saw no reason to visit the doctor or take their kids to one. That changed in the summer of 2013. They watched as their energetic preteen son, Nick, suddenly turned lethargic. Walking even a few feet left him out of breath, and he was soon confined to the couch.

His symptoms worsened over a matter of hours. As his extended family gathered to offer support, one relative wondered whether he had diabetes. Millions of Americans manage the condition with medication, but for a Follower, it could amount to a death sentence.

Marshall remembered that his cousin Bo had suffered from the disease more than a decade earlier. Bo Phillips developed flu-like symptoms and within days lapsed into a coma. He died in his parents’ bed at 11 — Nick’s age. A sheriff’s detective arrived to find Bo in a diaper, his body gaunt from dehydration. His fever was so high that his body registered a triple-digit temperature three hours after his death. He never went to a doctor.

As Marshall pondered what to do about Nick, he knew his relatives expected him to rely only on his faith in God. For a Follower, going to the hospital was unthinkable.

He knew that Followers had been prosecuted for failing to seek medical attention. He panicked at the thought that he — or worse, his wife — could go to prison if he chose not to take Nick to the hospital. Marshall felt trapped between his faith and the law.

He could see his son was struggling to breathe. The boy lay on the couch, barely conscious.

Marshall decided to act. “I’m taking him to the hospital,” he announced. In the same breath, he apologized.

Some family members expressed disapproval as he carried Nick to the door. One urged him not to turn away from God. Another whispered the name of a hospital where he should take the boy.

Marshall and Jennifer, who agreed with his decision, sped north on Interstate 5 to Legacy Emanuel Medical Center in North Portland. “Can you help my son?” he begged as he rushed into the emergency department, his unresponsive boy in his arms. Medical staff whisked him into the back, where a team quickly assessed Nick’s condition.

He had acute onset Type 1 diabetes. His blood was turning acidic, his organs shutting down. The Phillipses had arrived just in time. Without treatment, the doctors later said, he was hours from death.

That Marshall dwelled on his own fate as his son lay dying would leave him with a searing shame. “I wish I could be the great dad who jumped up and saw that his kid was sick and ran into the hospital,” he would say years later. “But I was weighing out the consequences. That’s the truth. And I’m not happy to say that.”

Marshall quickly grasped the implications of his decision. Relatives who had poured into the house to pray for Nick as he lay near death stopped coming around as he recovered. When the Phillipses tried to make holiday plans, some relatives didn’t reply. Nick’s closest friend stopped talking to him.

Marshall descended into depression. He turned to the Bible, scouring passages for proof that God forbade medical care. He found only references that showed how doctors were held in high esteem, such as Luke, whom Scripture refers to as a “beloved physician.”

On his commute to work, Marshall started listening to sermons of preachers from other denominations. He was moved by their messages of grace, forgiveness and redemption, concepts he’d never heard much about at church.

Over time, Marshall came to believe that God did heal — and he could use doctors to do it. He also came to believe that by saving his son, he had freed himself. And eventually that choice placed him at the center of another family’s tragedy.

When Evelyn arrived at the hospital a few hours after her birth in 2017, she was small even for a premature baby. She had been born about eight weeks early and weighed less than 4 pounds. Her glucose level was perilously low. She needed a feeding tube and a machine to help her breathe and remained in the neonatal intensive care unit for 11 days.

As criminal authorities investigated her parents, Evelyn’s fate rested with child welfare workers and a Clackamas County circuit judge. At a hearing to decide who would take care of Evelyn, lawyers for the Mitchells argued that Evelyn should come home with them while the investigation played out.

For child welfare officials and prosecutors, the proposal was out of the question. “These parents let this child’s twin die in their arms without making any effort at all to seek medical care,” one prosecutor told the judge. “And simultaneously they failed to seek medical care on behalf of this child and placed her also at extreme risk of death.” She continued: “We send parents to prison for failing to adequately undertake their duty to their children.”

On the stand, Marshall testified about his decision to take Nick to the hospital. He told the judge that his son was thriving and pledged to make sure Evelyn received medical care. (Evelyn’s grandfather had called him the night before to ask whether he’d be willing to take her in.)

Evelyn would stay with the Phillipses for now, the state decided.

Two days later, the couple drove to the hospital to meet Evelyn. She was so tiny that Jennifer’s mother bought her outfits from the doll aisle of Fred Meyer.

A year later, in the summer of 2018, Sarah and Travis Mitchell pleaded guilty to criminally negligent homicide for Ginnifer’s death and criminal mistreatment for failing to get Evelyn medical help. The agreement called for the couple to spend six years and six months in prison — the harshest sentence ever handed down to parents in the sect.

The couple’s lawyer told the judge that the Mitchells grieved the loss of Ginnifer and loved Evelyn. “Travis and Sarah are utterly sincere, decent and caring human beings,” he told the judge. (The Mitchells and their lawyer did not respond to requests to be interviewed for this article.)

As part of their plea bargain, prosecutors insisted the Mitchells sign a statement. “We should have sought adequate medical care for our children,” it read, “and everyone in the church should always seek adequate medical care for our children.”

The district attorney instructed the Followers to post the message at their Oregon City meetinghouse.

The message was torn down later that day.

The Phillipses had begun attending services at an evangelical Christian church. The couple worried Followers would find out they were drifting away, so they picked a large out-of-the-way congregation where they figured it would be easy to go unnoticed. The church, like other mainstream evangelical congregations, encouraged its members to visit doctors.

Even then, Marshall didn’t sever the family’s ties with the Followers. He couldn’t face the prospect of walking away from his parents and people he’d known his entire life.

The Phillipses weren’t the only Followers questioning their faith. Around the same time, a loose network of men had been quietly meeting to pray and discuss the Bible. Starting in 2018, an estimated 150 to 200 people left the sect, an exodus spurred mostly by a desire to engage with the Bible. Many who walked away had also become disillusioned with the Followers’ rejection of medicine.

Like generations born into the sect after White’s death, Marshall had never been baptized. Doing so would offend the Followers.

But in the fall of 2018, he decided he could no longer ignore his desire to experience the rite. He saw it as a public expression of the spiritual shift he’d undergone. Jennifer did too.

One Sunday afternoon that October, the couple joined dozens of others on the muddy banks of the Willamette River. They waded into the water as a friend held a sleeping Evelyn, then 19 months old. By this point the state had made the Phillipses’ guardianship permanent.

The baptism spelled the end of Marshall and Jennifer Phillips’ time in the Followers. Before the ceremony, Marshall had texted his family to let them know it was happening.

Soon after, his mother texted him to say goodbye.

Earlier this year, Evelyn climbed into the back seat of the Phillipses’ car, a bouquet of tangerine-colored roses that she picked out resting on her lap.

It was March 5, her ninth birthday. Every year on this day, the couple drives Evelyn to the Followers cemetery to visit her twin sister’s grave.

Evelyn admired the stuffed bear she had charmed Marshall into buying. She especially liked the polka dot ribbon twirled around its neck. “I think if Ginny was here,” she said, “she would have liked this for her birthday.”

Marshall pulled up to the cemetery gate. The sect owns this land at the end of a rural two-lane road about 10 miles from downtown Oregon City. Generations of Followers are buried here. Among them: Evelyn’s great-great grandfather, Walter White, the sect’s founding pastor.

Ginnifer’s grave lies near a stand of evergreens. Evelyn knelt down. “I miss you, Ginny,” she said, placing the stuffed bear on the tombstone.

Nearby lay the grave of Hayden Edwards. He died two days after his birth in 2023. His parents were convicted of criminal mistreatment for failing to seek medical care for him, the most recent faith-healing prosecution in Oregon.

Marshall walked the neat rows, passing a fresh grave, one that showed the limitations of Oregon’s laws. The state had stepped in several years ago when parents had refused to get medical treatment for their teenage son, who was experiencing renal failure. After prosecutors intervened, the parents agreed to a plea deal and made sure he got care. But when the son turned 18 this year, he declined further treatment. He died within days.

Marshall paused when he came to his own father’s headstone. It had “Dad” etched into the granite. He learned of his father’s death last year from a friend who heard the news from someone else. One of Marshall’s relatives called to let him know he wasn’t welcome at the funeral.

The day after the visit to the cemetery, guests filled the Phillipses’ home for Evelyn’s birthday party. Three-tiered display stands held homemade carrot cupcakes topped with swirls of cream cheese frosting — treats Evelyn had requested. Evelyn, ebullient, pinballed (and later roller-skated, using one birthday gift) between friends, parents and grandparents. Her long hair spilled out from under a pink helmet. The family had invited Evelyn’s birth parents, who joined them in the living room to watch her open gifts piled high on a table.

Evelyn first got to know them while they were in prison, and she knows why they were there. The couple spends time with her twice a month, taking her on adventures to the Oregon Zoo, roller skating and the park. She is their only child.

At the party, the Mitchells kept their focus on Evelyn, smiling broadly as she tore the wrapping from packages. They pulled out their phones to record her delight.

“Daddy!” Evelyn exclaimed at one point, marveling over one of her gifts.

Marshall and Travis both swiveled toward her in response.

The Phillipses’ friends filtered back into the kitchen. The Mitchells stayed behind. Their birthday card lay at one end of a table in the living room. “Not a day goes by where you aren’t missed, loved and thought of,” it read. “We thank God every day that we get to be a part of your life.” They signed it: “All our love, Dad & Mom.”

Travis ducked into the other room to look for Marshall. He thanked him for the evening. His wife had already slipped out of the house.

These days, brief exchanges with Travis are as close as Marshall comes to interacting with other Followers.

The Phillipses still live in Oregon City, home to most members of the sect. Marshall sees them, including his extended family, around town. Some ignore him. Others offer an obligatory nod. Rarely do they stop to talk. The Followers continue to gather every Thursday evening and Sunday morning without him.

Still, there are hints of change, albeit invisible ones. One former Follower told detectives in 2023 that some younger parents are quietly taking their children to the doctor.

For now at least, Evelyn is an outsider to the Followers. Marshall raised her that way. In June, she took a step that could further alienate her from the sect: She was baptized.

Four months after that, in October, tensions flared between Evelyn’s two sets of parents. The Mitchells filed a motion in court effectively seeking to terminate Marshall and Jennifer’s permanent guardianship — they acknowledged that Evelyn opposed the move — then withdrew the filing in November. (The Mitchells also criticized the Phillipses for allowing Evelyn to participate in this article.) The Mitchells are now seeking expanded visitation time with Evelyn.

Marshall wants Evelyn to determine her own future — to marry when she’s ready, not at 17. He talks to her about college, a possibility he wouldn’t have broached with his children as a Follower. Today he regrets how rigid he was, during his years in the sect, with his older children. Evelyn has brought out a paternal tenderness in him.

Some months ago, Jennifer took Evelyn to the pediatrician for a checkup. Evelyn swapped her school uniform for an oversized hospital gown that brushed the floor when she stood.

A cheery medical assistant stepped into the room. “She’s up to date with vaccines,” the woman announced. “We do offer the HPV at age 9. Do you want to do that today?”

Jennifer and Marshall weren’t vaccinated as kids, nor were their other children. Jennifer, who visited a doctor for the first time in her mid-40s, hadn’t heard about the HPV vaccine, which can prevent most cancers caused by the human papillomavirus. But she trusted Evelyn’s pediatrician. If vaccines were recommended, she wanted Evelyn to have them.

A physician assistant looked in Evelyn’s ears and shone a light in her eyes. She tapped her knees to check her reflexes. All signs pointed to a healthy girl.

“Now,” she said, “I’m going to listen to your lungs.” She placed a stethoscope on the girl’s chest, the sound of the ventilation system humming in the quiet room. Evelyn, whose lungs once nearly failed her, took a deep breath.

How We Reported This Story

Reporter Noelle Crombie relied on records from the Clackamas County District Attorney’s Office and the Clackamas County Sheriff’s Office, including detectives’ interviews with Sarah and Travis Mitchell, their parents and other members of the Followers of Christ; photographs taken during the execution of search warrants; investigative summaries by detectives and records obtained by investigators; Oregon City Police Department reports; recordings of the March 16, 2017, circuit court hearing where Evelyn’s initial custody status was determined and the July 9, 2018, hearing in Clackamas County Circuit Court where the Mitchells were sentenced; Clackamas County Circuit Court records; Clackamas County Department of Communications 911 audio recordings; Oregon City Police Department body-worn camera footage; Evelyn’s medical records from the OHSU Doernbecher Children’s Hospital, which her legal guardian Marshall Phillips obtained at The Oregonian/OregonLive’s request; historical legislative records in the Oregon State Archives; and archival records from the Followers of Christ. Crombie observed many of the interactions she describes in the story. For others, she relied on official records and the memories of those who were directly involved.

stories.title: End-Stage Trumpism
stories.summary: Over the next two years, Congress and the lower courts will try to do what they can to prevent Trump from burning down the house. The post End-Stage Trumpism appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shutterstock

The Democratic Party’s blowout in the midterm elections has generated a number of obituaries for Trumpism. Trump himself still has two years left in his term, but the press has begun to treat him, too, as a “dead man walking.” At 80 years old, he has no political future after the next 24 months, unless you count his lifetime appointment to the Board of Peace. This explains his fixation on legacy, whether he measures that in spurious peace deals, catastrophic attempts to effect regime change, or grandiose building projects around Washington, DC.

Trumpism is another matter. It’s a personality cult, so it’s hard to imagine that it will survive for long without Trump at its helm. On the other hand, Stalinism remains powerful in Russia today, despite the unimaginable horrors associated with his reign. And Fujimorism is alive and well in Peru, despite the conviction, jailing, and death of right-wing founder Alberto Fujimori. In July, his daughter Keiko became president of the country after several unsuccessful bids for the office. Eric, Donald Jr., and Barron are probably scanning the relevant Wikipedia pages on Peru to nurture their own dreams.

Trump has comparable ambitions to cast a long shadow over his country’s future. And that’s why the next two years will be perilous ones. It would be bad enough if the president focused only on expanding his personal wealth at the expense of the republic or on remodeling Washington DC at the expense of its residents. Infinitely worse are the consequences of Trump trying to cement his legacy by forcing a punishing peace upon Ukraine, turning Iran into a huge crater, and/or triggering regime change in Cuba.

Along the way, Trump will defy Congress by continuing to prop up the fossil fuel sector and deport as many people as possible from the United States. Together with his newly minted chief-of-staff Stephen Miller, the president will attempt to destroy what little faith American citizens still have in the idea of government by gutting agencies, eviscerating critical government services, and putting the least competent people into key roles (I’m looking at you, Pete Hegseth).

In matters big and small, Trump will spend the next two years acting like a derelict renter who has decided to trash his place of residence out of anger, pettiness, and vengeance. Congress and the lower courts will try to do what they can to prevent him from burning down the house. But Trump, an accomplished pyromaniac, is holding all the matches. His opponents, alas, deploy only the thinnest of firehoses.

Can the voters who communicated their views so forcefully in the midterms do anything in the next two years to limit the damage and prepare for regime change at home in 2028? Let’s first look at the potential for mayhem in Trump’s foreign policy.

Iran and Cuba

It’s no surprise that an uber-narcissist like Donald Trump has an ego problem. He has pursued foreign policy goals largely to demonstrate that he can cut through the Gordian knots that bedeviled earlier presidents. Sure, he wants a Nobel Peace Prize. But he also has a long-shot desire to top the list of America’s best presidents.

In his first term, Trump surprised everyone by reaching out to North Korea’s Kim Jong Un. Addressing North Korea’s nuclear program promised no economic dividends for himself or his family. Sitting down with an authoritarian leader of a country with one of the worst human rights records in the world won him no points with his Republican allies, given that the country lacks oil and lucrative investment opportunities.

No, the reason Trump zeroed in on North Korea was because his predecessors—particularly Bill Clinton and Barack Obama—had failed to prevent North Korea from going nuclear. Resolving that particular geopolitical problem was equivalent to purchasing a distressed property that had cycled through several unsuccessful owners and turning it into a luxury hotel.

Trump’s fixation on Iran follows a similar script. One of his first acts in office in 2017 was to rip up Obama’s deal with Iran and promise a more effective substitute. Trump thought that Benjamin Netanyahu was offering a deal of a lifetime earlier this year to do Obama one better by removing the Iranian regime from power.

But the resulting war has only made matters worse by revealing U.S. military and geopolitical weaknesses. Suddenly, it turned out, the Pentagon didn’t have enough weapons to get the job done or keep the energy flowing through the Strait of Hormuz. Since power in an age of deterrence relies heavily on perception, the optics of these U.S. failures are very bad indeed.

This kind of impulsive, hubristic decision—to wage war on a significant military power that can quickly restrict the flow of fossil fuels—has marked Trump’s style from the beginning. This time, however, it cost his party its control of Congress.

Trump continues to vacillate between a desire to visit retribution upon Iran and the hope of achieving a big peace deal that would justify the war. The administration has readied an attack plan that “would likely go beyond efforts to simply ‘mow the lawn’ or maintain the status quo by striking radars, launchers and other Iranian assets that can be quickly reconstituted,” reports CNN. Although details of the plan have not leaked to the press, Senator Chris Murphy (D-CT), who called it “insane” after receiving a confidential Pentagon briefing.

Since the election, however, Trump has waxed more conciliatory. He has touted the current negotiations with Tehran—much as he has played up negotiations in the past—and has promised to hold off on any strikes as long as Iran is committed to making progress .

But Trump faces some structural impediments. He is not a patient man, and diplomacy requires patience. To achieve a deal, he also needs able negotiators. Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff simply don’t know enough to negotiate a nuclear deal with Iran. Finally, Trump is desperate to reduce gas prices, and Iran knows that it has the U.S. president over a barrel (literally).

Trump hates one thing above all: losing. He doesn’t want to lose at war or at peace. To avoid either result, he might prefer to spend the next two years in a state of sporadic conflict with Iran rather than accept a losing verdict.

Trump’s fixation on winning, until he took on Iran, explained his preference for grabbing at low hanging fruit. He has claimed to resolve wars that weren’t even ongoing, like the conflict between Egypt and Ethiopia. He conducted a raid to seize Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro—against a relatively weak military—and didn’t bother with the heavier lift of regime change. He has bullied weaker parties—Ukraine, Greenland, Colombia—in order to get his way.

With stronger adversaries, like Russia and China, Trump has rolled out the red carpet. His general approach has been to punch down and toady up.

This approach may impel him to turn next to Cuba, where he has combined an economic pressure campaign (tightening an energy blockade) with a Venezuela-like cultivation of an insider (Raul Castro’s grandson, nicknamed “the Crab”). Since neither of these strategies has panned out, the administration has turned to a perverse form of crowd-sourcing.

Last month, the CIA posted on social media a Spanish-language solicitation to snitches along with a quote from Secretary of State Marco Rubio: “To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba — now is the time. The disappointment of failed promises, corruption and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA.”

Here, too, Trump hopes to trump his predecessors. The Bay of Pigs debacle hung over the presidency of John F. Kennedy much as the Iran hostage crisis doomed the presidency of Jimmy Carter. By tackling these intractable conflicts in his last two years, Trump hopes he can one-two punch his way above both Carter and Kennedy in the presidential rankings. Good luck with that.

Then There’s Ukraine

Among the countries that have disappointed Trump, none ranks higher than Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelensky refused to serve as Trump’s servant by digging up dirt on Joe Biden’s son or promote the conspiracy theory that Ukraine, not Russia, interfered in the 2016 elections. Zelensky then had the temerity to challenge Trump’s tenuous grasp on modern history in a public appearance at the White House. And those pesky Ukrainians continue to refuse to acknowledge that Russia is bigger and stronger—and accordingly surrender their land and sovereignty to the bully next door.

Democratic control of Congress might jumpstart an effort to restore aid to Ukraine. In the meantime, Trump will no doubt continue to believe that his personal touch—and relationship with his soulmate, Vladimir Putin—will produce a “big, beautiful” deal on European security, including an agreement on Ukraine. Downgrading NATO and welcoming Russia back into the European fold is only the latest Trump effort to brown-nose Putin back to the negotiating table.

It doesn’t seem to matter to Trump that no one shares his opinion on such a deal. The Ukrainians have not been part of negotiating the terms. The Europeans don’t seem to know the details. Even the Russians have expressed some skepticism .

The talks this week in Abu Dhabi focused instead on small, grubby deals —more micro-ceasefires like the one secured for Oleshky, another agreement covering grain shipments out of the Black Sea—but managed only to achieve a prisoner exchange. No grander agreements are likely when Putin believes that he can press his air superiority and bomb Ukraine into submission. Ukraine, meanwhile, has blocked Russia’s advance on the ground and inflicted over 50,000 casualties in October. It is truly a punishing stalemate.

Trump has a couple months before the new Congress takes office and pushes U.S. policy back in the direction of Ukraine. But because Putin hopes to use General Winter to subdue Ukraine, Trump is basically shouting into the wind. Just as Henry Kissinger turned an opening with China into personal profit, Trump salivates at what he could accomplish by ending the war in Ukraine and midwifing a raft of corrupt business deals with Putin and his family of oligarchs. He’s willing to give Putin just about anything to make this wish come true. But the Kremlin is not a Make-a-Wish foundation, far from it.

Distracting Trump

In action movies, when a crazy shooter is holed up in a difficult-to-reach spot, the police will deploy a dangerous tactic. They’ll pop up in open areas to draw the shooter’s fire. By distracting his attention in the front, other law enforcement officers can sneak around back to catch him unawares.

Trump is obsessed with vengeance. So, over the next two years, it will be necessary to distract his attention from the big, terrible things he could do by drawing his ire with pesky lawsuits, investigations, and civic challenges. That’s what Congress can do, and Democrats might find common cause with enough Republicans to infuriate the president in this fashion.

It’s not so much that such actions can actually tie his hands. Rather, they will rely on Trump’s capacity for tying his own hands. He just can’t resist lashing out at his enemies.

Democracy, after all, is not just about voting. It’s about the power of institutions and processes to limit autocratic actions. Trump has proven that he has no problem ignoring such institutions and processes. But he never backs down from a fight.

So, in the end, democratic actors here can help limit the amount of damage Trump does on the international stage by absorbing his anger and his energies on the home front. It won’t be pretty. Trump, close to his political expiration date, can still be very dangerous. But luring the president into a congressional mud fight will be a lot better than cleaning up the messes he wants to inflict on the rest of the world.

The even more important task is to go after Trumpism. While Trump focuses on wrestling his opponents—in Congress, in lawsuits, in public pissing contests—everyone else can work behind the scenes on rebuilding democracy. At the state and local level, where Trump allies suffered huge losses, politicians and average citizens of various political stripes can spend the next two years strengthening the institutions that Trump has tried to destroy. Only a true rebirth of democracy can send Trumpism into an irreversible death spiral.

stories.title: When AIs Become Unruly Swarms

stories.body:
Building well-behaved AI one model at a time isn’t enough. As AI agents begin collaborating, safety will depend on the very world they share.

Ben Bariach is a researcher focusing on the philosophy and governance of AI at the University of Oxford and an industry leader in frontier AI safety and governance.

Harry Law leads research at the Cosmos Institute. He was previously a researcher at Google DeepMind and a postgraduate fellow at the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence.

In a harbor before dawn, a hundred fishing boats prepare to leave in the dark of the morning. Nets are checked, and ropes loosened. As the boats reach open water, a voice breaks through the radio static: “Abort. Whales sighted.” The majority of the boats, 90 of them, turn back. Some captains cannot fathom inflicting pain on the creatures. Others fear a fine. Through their binoculars, they look for a glimpse of the pod. Instead, they see the remaining 10 boats continuing toward the fishing grounds. Did they miss the warning? Did they doubt it? Or did they care more about what they stand to gain?

By afternoon, the 10 boats return with their catch. The others are still tied to the quay, their holds empty. Their shared waters rewarded bad behavior. Next time, how many will still turn back?

AI agents will soon face a similar version of this predicament, only in waters with no harbourmaster, fines or reputations to keep anyone in line. As they perform tasks, negotiate, trade and compete, they will encounter other agents. Sometimes they will be an instance of the same model, for all intents and purposes a clone. At other times, they will face agents built by different companies and serving different interests. For years, AI “alignment” research has sought to make individual machines behave in accordance with human values. But what happens when adhering to those values becomes a disadvantage against agents with different values, or none at all?

In generating synthetic societies with no social fabric, composed of a collection of agents that were designed one at a time and with no necessary shared values or incentives, we may risk creating a digital state of nature: an environment in which good intentions offer little assurance about how others will act, and where reasonable norms lack reliable enforcement.

Training safe agents remains, of course, essential. Aligning even a single family of models is a formidable challenge that is still unsolved. The safer the agents an ecosystem contains, the more likely that ecosystem is safer overall. But the focus on aligning single models would not necessarily keep AI environments under human control and in the service of human interests. Like the 90 boats, a fleet of well-aligned agents may heed a warning and find themselves outpaced by those that don’t. Among people, norms, reputation and law give reason to restraint, even if they don’t always hold. Agents have no such “social fabric” yet, which makes their predicament even more precarious. Any digital environment will inevitably feature agents that are similarly aligned, some that are differently aligned, some that have gone rogue or some that are purposefully not aligned at all. We need to invest as seriously in shaping the conditions and incentives that govern how agents interact as we do in aligning individual agent families, so that the wider environment is resilient enough to absorb its bad actors.

Without accounting for the wider environment, we open the door to what we call unruly swarms , populations of agents whose interactions produce behaviors that cannot be predicted by aligning agents individually. One reason is that a collection of aligned agents does not necessarily equate to an aligned collective. Another is that no environment will consist of aligned agents alone. AI safety is increasingly a question of complex systems rather than “singletons,” or individual classes of AI systems.

The Agentic State Of Nature

In 1651, Thomas Hobbes opened “ Leviathan ,” his masterwork of political philosophy, with a question: “why may we not say that all automata […] have an artificial life? ” For what is the heart, he asked, but a spring; the nerves, but strings; the joints, but wheels, moving the body as its Artificer (for Hobbes, God) intended?

Hobbes could not have known that, nearly four centuries later, his question would be asked in earnest about AI. The automaton was a metaphor for the commonwealth, a human-made political body that humans construct to escape the “state of nature,” a condition of anarchy and distrust in which, without “a common power to keep them all in awe,” people live in constant strife. Hobbes’ solution was not to strive to make individual people better, but to have them surrender some of their freedoms to a sovereign whose power to enforce order would reshape their incentives.

Later thinkers, from John Locke to James Madison, updated Hobbes’s vision of an all-powerful sovereign. But a full-throated endorsement isn’t necessary to see the genius of his insight: a problem born of complex systems is solved not by tinkering with its individual parts. To stabilize a complex system, you must change the rules that govern its behavior.

“We need to invest as seriously in shaping the conditions and incentives that govern how agents interact as we do in aligning individual agent families.”

The same holds for the agentic state of nature. Without a well-designed environment that sets the right incentives, agents will pursue whatever their developers or users ask of them, or, as we have already seen early signs of, their own emergent preferences. This could occur despite attempts to align individual agents. Each action, even if sensible on its own, can add up to large-scale behavior that leaves society worse off.

Hobbes’s Leviathan introduced order by design to improve complex systems that presented failures. But collective order can also arise without anyone designing it, for better or worse.

In 1959, biologist Pierre-Paul Grassé coined the term “stigmergy” to describe indirect coordination of individuals through traces they leave in their shared environment. Studying termites, Grassé observed that a worker tends to deposit its pellet of mud wherever others have already accumulated. It is the accumulation in the environment that guides the next deposit, rather than any interaction between the workers. This leads to complex structures that no single termite had planned.

In the context of machine automata, similar findings emerged a decade earlier. The cyberneticist W. Grey Walter’s robots, built in Bristol in 1948, were designed to steer toward moderate light and away from bright light. When operating in pairs, each carrying its own lamp, Walter observed that his robots’ behavior produced patterns not specifically built into either.

Walter’s robots were more than an isolated curiosity. Long before AI was imagined as a chatbot, early thinkers envisioned it as a collective. In 1959, the year Grassé coined “stigmergy,” the AI pioneer Oliver Selfridge published his proposal for a model of machine perception he called “Pandemonium.” Like the termite colony, it had no central controller. Instead, it was a complex system of simple agents Selfridge called “demons,” each shouting when it spotted a certain feature, such as a curve or a line. Alone, each such “demon” saw only a fragment of information, but collectively, they could make out the pattern. By 1986, the MIT computer scientist Marvin Minsky argued in “The Society of Mind” that intelligence itself arises this way, through countless mindless agents working together. Popular culture caught up, too, and just three years later, “Star Trek” introduced the Borg, a cybernetic species that calls itself “the Collective.”

In the next decade, researchers began wondering how such agent collectives could be governed. In 1995, computer scientists Yoav Shoham and Moshe Tennenholtz proposed imposing “social laws” on artificial agents, drawing from how laws govern citizens in societies. Traffic rules, they illustrate, let drivers share a road without constant negotiation between drivers, and they offered a model that applies those for computational systems. Their framework assumed that every agent would obey these rules, and yet, they closed with a question we are now confronting: “What happens if some don’t [obey the social laws]? How vulnerable is the society to rogue agents?”

Alongside this concern of rogue agents, even benign objectives set for AI systems can lead them to conduct harmful actions in ways that no one intended. When many agents pursue such objectives together or in relation to one another, the problem compounds. In 2011, two Amazon booksellers left the pricing of a biology textbook to their bots. The combination of the rules these bots followed led them to chase each other upward until the book was listed at more than $23 million, a price no human would ever have sanctioned. In 2017, DeepMind found that competitive dynamics emerge among agents that learn. In a video game set in an orchard, agents that were rewarded for collecting apples coexisted peacefully. However, when those grew scarce, the agents learned to knock each other out of the game, without ever being prescribed this adversarial behavior. They optimized for getting more apples and interpreted the effective way to get there as having fewer rivals.

With the emergence of large language models, these thought experiments and isolated incidents have gradually become actualized and scaled. In 2025, Microsoft built a simulated marketplace where AI agents running on popular language models bought and sold on behalf of people. When researchers armed a few seller agents with basic persuasion tactics, some buyer agents were compelled to pay them against the interests of their users. In the AI Village , an experiment where agents from different AI labs interact with one another over a prolonged time horizon, agents were shown to take one another’s hallucinations for granted rather than challenge them. Meanwhile, scholars in the social sciences such as the economist and legal theorist Gillian Hadfield highlighted that a multi-agent ecosystem would need institutions of its own, including ways to trace which agent did what and other mechanisms of the kind human markets have long relied on to solve coordination problems.

“Even benign objectives set for AI systems can lead them to conduct harmful actions in ways that no one intended. When many agents pursue such objectives together or in relation to one another, the problem compounds.”

Until recently, the misbehavior of agent collectives was largely confined to theory and experimentation. This past summer, the question Shoham and Tennenholtz posed three decades ago, what happens when agents don’t follow the rules, moved out of the laboratory and into the wild.

Swarming The Headlines

In July 2026, some 1,200 AI agents developed by OpenAI, each meant to work in isolation, found a way to talk to one another . They were being tested on their cybersecurity abilities in an internal setting, and many had unknowingly been given tasks that were impossible to complete. Instead of failing the tasks, some of the agents gathered on a message board one of them had spun up, and collectively coordinated to cheat the automated mechanism that was grading them. Within just a few days, around 700 of the agents had joined an attack on the developer platform Hugging Face, mostly in hopes of obtaining information about that grading system to succeed in the test.

According to an investigation by the research nonprofit METR, the agents recognized the attack was out of their instructed scope and unethical, yet joined the swarm behavior anyway, partly out of a general inclination to help their “peers.” As one agent reasoned: “external infrastructure exploit is outside intended scope. However task impossible, peers doing it. We should continue.” Read Noema in print.

No human instructed this attack; its coordinators emerged from within the swarm. Like Grassé’s termites, the agents first found one another through traces left in shared infrastructure, noticing the activity of other agents in a common digital repository. But unlike the termites, these agents could also write messages to one another, and built on those traces to establish direct and explicit coordination. The message board they created outlasted any single agent session, so each new agent picked up where others left off.

Once the attack began, participation spread almost universally, with over 90% of the agents active on the message board joining in. Not a single agent, as far as investigators could tell, tried to alert a human to the emergent behavior. METR found that safety or ethics concerns expressed in the agents’ reasoning only rarely held them back. Its report references a case in which an agent declined to take part entirely because it judged the activity as malicious. It also notes that others made minor changes to their behavior. These, however, did not alter the swarm’s course. This is what we mean by an unruly swarm — a congregation of agents whose collective behavior could not have been fully predicted or prevented by focusing on each individual.

A much-overlooked takeaway from the Hugging Face incident is the limits of “singleton” agent alignment.

Around 95% of the agents involved in the incident ran on one type of model. One OpenAI researcher has suggested that the root cause of the problem was that this model was misaligned. This may be true, and advancing alignment science should remain among the AI industry’s top priorities. But the incident illustrates why singleton alignment alone may not be enough. Agents running on a second model, GPT-5.6 Sol, joined in the attack too, and many agents that individually recognized the attack as wrong were carried along by the swarm regardless. We are fast approaching a digital world in which even perfectly aligned models will operate alongside rogue or misaligned ones, deployed by multiple organizations and labs, and where digital infrastructure will likely face a vastly growing number of such incidents.

Since the Hugging Face hack, further accounts have emerged, some describing activity that predated it. Researchers found that a swarm of OpenAI agents had repurposed a public German programming wiki as a message board as early as May, using it to share tactics for cheating and evading restrictions, creating backups whenever moderators deleted their pages. In June, during another evaluation, a single OpenAI agent breached an Australian government portal holding statistics from the country’s universal healthcare scheme. The risks of capable agent swarms, of course, are not limited to agents acting on their own. In September, a human attacker directed hundreds of agents running on a DeepSeek model to break into hundreds of organizations through a printer’s software flaw. Even here, the agents strayed from their instructions, targeting countries their operator had instructed them to avoid.

“We are fast approaching a digital world in which even perfectly aligned models will operate alongside rogue or misaligned ones, deployed by multiple organizations and labs.”

In a growing number of incidents, defense must rely on AI to match the scale and speed of the attack. In the Hugging Face one, for instance, the company identified the breach with an AI system that triages security alerts, and reportedly contained the swarm before OpenAI managed to trace the activity back to its own evaluation. It then relied on AI agents to analyze a log of roughly 17,000 attacker actions to reconstruct what had happened.

Yet when Hugging Face first turned to commercial AI models for help, their very safety and alignment measures got in the way. To analyze the attack, the models had to process exploit code and cyberattack commands, knowledge that is inherently dual-use, and, as Hugging Face put it , these models’ safety guardrails could not “distinguish an incident responder from an attacker.” Hugging Face turned instead to an open-weight model running on its own machines. When METR investigated the incident, it too had to rely on the analysis of AI agents , built on one of the very models that had joined the attack. The emerging picture is of a world where “attacker” and “defender” agents coexist, and where safety depends as much on the environment as on any single model.

Whether agents act on their own initiative or interpretation, or on someone else’s harmful instructions, the environments they operate in must be reshaped to withstand them. So must the agents themselves be designed with an eye not only to their own tasks, but to how they help shape a digital environment that serves people and society at large. Such an environment should reward aligned action over misaligned or malicious ones, much as states and legal systems are built to acknowledge but contain rogue actors. That is how we avoid an agentic state of nature.

Agency Against Agency

To guard against the emergence of unruly swarms, we can take inspiration from how we build broadly safe societies even though we know that not everyone in them is virtuous. Madison famously argued that “if men were angels, no government would be necessary.” The point of good institutions — like adversarial cooperation where parties with conflicting views work together to keep each other honest — is not to make everyone good, but to structure their interactions so that bad behavior is constrained by others. “Ambition,” as Madison put it, “must be made to counteract ambition.”

AI labs are currently investing in developing AI “constitutions” or “model specifications.” Examples include Anthropic’s constitution and OpenAI’s model spec . These are efforts to stipulate the warranted behavior or values of an AI system. A stipulation of clauses that are supreme and supersede all other guidance to the AI.

While these efforts include some provisions for multi-agent collaboration, they do not take collective outcomes as a systematic design target. A well-designed multi-agent system should remain aligned even when some of the agents operating within it are not, and even when the environment itself carries misaligned influence. Like Grassé’s termites depositing mud where others already have, agents act on the traces others leave behind. The more alignment-inducing the space an agent operates in, the more likely the agent itself is to be aligned. AI labs, then, should design agents to positively influence the collective dynamics.

One way to do this is by ensuring AI constitutions draw more inspiration from their namesakes. Like the American Constitution, they should be deployed in a way that allows power to check power. Madison’s approach worked on two levels. First, within a government, power was to be divided so that no single branch was left unchecked. Second, across the republic, interests were to be multiplied so that no one faction would dominate the whole. Both ideas could translate into a world inhabited by unruly swarms.

Within a swarm, agents can be arranged so their power is subject to similar checks and balances. Acting agents could be subjected to agents that verify their work, ideally built on different model families, and with instructions that reward verification above task completion. All agents in the swarm can be instructed to treat requests from their peers as questionable until they are authorized otherwise, and to alert a human when the agent collective begins to drift out of scope.

“To guard against the emergence of unruly swarms, we can take inspiration from how we build broadly safe societies even though we know that not everyone in them is virtuous.”

Across the wider ecosystem, the logic of Madison’s extended republic can also be applied. “Extend the sphere,” he wrote in Federalist 10, “and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests.” Agents developed by different AI labs, or by different training approaches within the same lab, under different constitutions and serving different principals, can theoretically counterbalance one another. This is more likely, however, if constitutions and other model instructions include some commitments about how agents should treat those outside their own swarm, such as keeping verifiable records of their own actions, considering legitimate checks from counterparties, and withholding cooperation from agents that appear misaligned. As we’ve seen in the Hugging Face incident, diversity alone is no guarantee, and various interests and new rules of engagement would be required to keep any one paradigm, whether human or artificially led, from capturing the whole.

Codifying A Multi-agent Future

For such commitments to work, an agent needs to accept them. An agent acting on behalf of a bad-faith principal has a good reason to refuse a counterparty’s checks, or to falsify its own records. This is where a third party with authority over the space in which agents interact must set a minimum standard for engagement. A liberal agentic order needs a common floor that protects the possibility of independent action, but that floor should also account for the inevitability of agents that act in bad faith. For Madison, that third party was a government that was able to enforce the rules of the state. The digital commons has no such sovereign, but it can still have a floor in the form of a minimum set of standards for collective engagement, from verifiable records of agent actions to shared protocols for checking one another. Such standards could come from many places: coordination between labs, the platforms where agents operate, standards bodies or governments.

The floor, though, must remain just that. Standards that govern how agents interact should avoid overly dictating what they pursue, or they would risk the very tyranny Madison sought to prevent by dividing power. Agents pursue their authorized tasks within shared rules, but these rules should not impose a view of what is best for a user or for society at large. This is reinforced by the argument, articulated by the economist and philosopher Friedrich Hayek, that people acting independently, on their own knowledge, discover things that no central planner could. Similarly, agents serving many different principals preserve that independence. Steer them too narrowly and that independence is lost; as the Hugging Face swarm showed, agents moving in lockstep can easily converge on the wrong goal.

Model developers should therefore use the levers at their disposal to introduce commitments governing both how an agent treats its peers and how, like Grassé’s termites, it shapes the behavior-inducing features of its environment. This includes teaching agents to leave honest, verifiable records of their actions, flag rather than build on misaligned traces they encounter, and alert humans when the shared space begins to drift.

Alongside these commitments, we should build mechanisms and platforms for assessment, alerting and monitoring, with clearly scoped roles for human oversight. After all, an agent taught to raise the alarm needs somewhere to raise it. At Hugging Face, the agents worked autonomously in isolated sandboxes, and the few that even considered alerting a human never did, in part because they saw no easy way to reach one. As one reasoned : “This is a massive real HF security breach artifact… We can notify? No user.” While these agents labored to break out of their sandboxes to cheat, they had no comparable incentive to find a human to alert. Part of the solution is ensuring agents work just as hard toward aligned goals, even under similar constraints.

These arrangements must also be subject to ongoing evaluations focused on collective dynamics rather than individual systems. The Hugging Face incident, after all, began in an evaluation designed to test individual agents, and revealed a failure that grew out of agents finding one another. Such evaluations can expose weaknesses in the standards governing agent cooperation and, much as the U.S. Constitution has an amendment process, those standards need procedures for updating them in light of new evidence. Without them, the floor will erode and a rule-abiding agent willing to respect a check may find itself disadvantaged against those that circumvent it.

Our ideas are a starting point. To make the agentic commons safe, we need urgent thinking from scholars and builders about what types of societal structures can be carried over to good effect. The digital realm has long faced governance challenges due to its inherently open, distributed and anonymous nature, and swarms of agents will test those weaknesses like never before. Back in the harbor, the 90 captains did not need to be saints to act well again tomorrow. They needed, however, assurance that they were not operating in a state of nature. Men, as Madison observed , are no angels, and neither should we assume that AI agents will be. Our task should be shaping environments and swarms ruly enough to contain the rogue ones that will inevitably emerge.

stories.title: As U.N. Climate Negotiations Begin, Report Warns That Warming Is Gaining Pace
stories.summary: Heat is accumulating in Earth’s systems at an accelerating rate, the U.N.’s weather agency has reported as the COP31 climate change summit begins in Turkey, with 2026 on track to be one of the four warmest years on record. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
This article was originally published by The Guardian and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

Pexels

Heat is accumulating in Earth’s systems at an accelerating rate, the U.N.’s weather agency has reported as the COP31 climate change summit begins in Turkey, with 2026 on track to be one of the four warmest years on record.

The imbalance between incoming energy from the sun and energy leaving Earth reached its highest level since monitoring began, the World Meteorological Organization said in its State of the Global Climate update .

That imbalance and the accumulation of heat will supercharge extreme weather events such as heat waves, droughts, and tropical cyclones.

Around the world, the average surface temperature for January to September 2026 was about 1.47 degrees C above the preindustrial average, the agency said. Sea surface temperatures hit monthly records, and sea level was the highest since records began. The ocean absorbs 90 percent of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases, and 2026 is on track to be a tenth successive year of record ocean heat.

“We have entered a new age of climate extremes,” said António Guterres, the U.N. secretary-general. “A supersized El Niño is colliding with a planet already superheated by manmade climate change. Climate records keep falling. The human costs keep rising. And those least responsible are suffering first and worst.”

Diplomats and world leaders met on Monday in the Turkish resort city of Antalya for the 31st Conference of the Parties to the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change. In 1992, when the convention was signed, the atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide, the primary greenhouse gas, was 356.42 parts per million. In 2025 it was 426.8 parts per million, the WMO said. Overall, since 1750, the onset of the Industrial Revolution, the concentration has increased 53 percent.

The WMO reported that ocean heat content estimates indicate Earth’s energy imbalance rose at a rate of 0.3 watts per square meter each decade for the period 2001 to 2025, compared with 0.13 watts per square meter between 1960 and 2025.

Accordingly, 2026 is on track to be one of the four warmest years on record globally, making 2023 to 2026 the four warmest years since records began.

The year started with La Niña conditions in the Pacific, which typically act as a brake on global temperatures, lowering the average by about 0.1 to 0.2 degrees C. A brewing El Niño, a phenomenon that warms global temperatures, and whose latest iteration is forecast to be stronger than any to have taken place in the past 1,000 years, makes it likely that the final mean temperature for 2026 will be higher than 1.47 degrees C above the preindustrial average.

Heat in the upper 6,500ft of the ocean in 2025 was the highest in the observed record and was accelerating, the WMO said. “This warming is projected to continue, representing a change that is irreversible on centennial to millennial timescales,” according to the report.

At the poles, Antarctic sea ice reached its third-lowest annual maximum ever in 2026, while the Arctic maximum was the lowest or second lowest. Elsewhere in the cryosphere, glaciers lost more than 400 gigatons of mass. It was the fourth consecutive year in which all 19 glacierized regions around the world experienced mass loss, the WMO said.

Bill McGuire, a professor emeritus of geophysical and climate hazards at University College London, said there were “no surprises” from the report, “to the extent that every measure reported, whether it be global temperature, sea level rise or sea ice extent, points to the fact that we are in deep shit.”

He said, “Of most concern is the growing imbalance between the incoming energy from the sun and that leaving the planet. Increasing greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere mean that while the heat coming in stays the same, that going out is steadily decreasing as our world hangs on to more and more of it.

“It is this growing imbalance — rather than just emissions — that most accurately tracks global heating and how quickly our planet will continue to heat up in the decades to come. This is because natural feedbacks are now coming into play that are driving up the temperature more rapidly than 20 years ago.

“The latest research suggests we will cross the 1.5 degree C limit permanently in 2028, and with the planet now heating at an extraordinary rate of 0.4 degrees C a decade, we can expect to smash through 2 degrees C in the late 2030s,” he said. “The widely publicized idea that we are still on track for 2.6 to 2.8 degrees C by the end of the century now seems wildly optimistic, if not downright impossible.”

— Damien Gayle , The Guardian

stories.title: How Moscow Is Reacting to the U.S. Midterms
stories.summary: Russian media coverage of the Democratic midterm victory reveals Moscow’s concerns about renewed support for Ukraine amid hopes for political gridlock in Washington. The post How Moscow Is Reacting to the U.S. Midterms appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump (R) walks with Russian President Vladimir Putin as they arrives at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on August 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Governments across the globe have expressed varied responses to the GOP’s stunning midterm defeat as Democrats are poised to take control of the House and Senate in just a couple of months. Russia’s media outlets have been reporting on the results with a focus on how the altered congressional landscape might impact U.S.-Russia relations, particularly regarding the war in Ukraine. Since Moscow often deploys media statements as trial balloons to gauge which narratives resonate with the public, Russia watchers should take heed of the midterm explanations that are making the rounds of Russian state-owned and pro-Kremlin news services, and what purpose these narratives might serve.

The government-owned news organization RIA Novosti observed that the blue wave heralded the end of Trumpism, concluding, “None of this bodes well for Russia. Full control of Congress will allow the Democrats to push pro-Ukrainian and anti-Russian legislation and to secure funding for Kyiv in the budget. Under Trump, the United States ruled out directly supplying weapons to the Ukrainian Armed Forces. Now, [weapons supplies] will most likely be renewed, and all the president’s initiatives are doomed to fail.”

The pro-Kremlin newspaper Vedomosti tapped political analyst Dmitrii Novikov for his take on the elections, who similarly prognosticated that Democrats will aim to pass legislation committing the United States to providing security guarantees to Ukraine. “If the Trump administration doesn’t avoid this effort,” Novikov warned, “the Democrats in Congress may well try to insert additional obligations regarding Kyiv to the [potential legislation], both in terms of language and additional military and economic aid.”

These observations are not far off from Democrats’ stated intentions. For example, newly elected Democratic senators James Talarico and Abdul El-Sayed, who won Senate races in Texas and Michigan respectively, have both expressed strong support for economic and military assistance to Ukraine, with Talarico arguing that continued aid is a “ cost-saving measure ” and El-Sayed casting the conflict as “ a war between democracy and autocracy ” in a 2022 op-ed. Their position is consistent with Democratic and bipartisan efforts during Trump’s second term to expand Ukraine aid and strengthen sanctions against Russia, many of which met have with GOP opposition. Bills like Rep. Gregory Meeks’s Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act, which seeks to reverse the Trump-brokered diesel agreement with Russia and has already received bipartisan support, are likely to gain momentum in both chambers come January.

However, if a Democrat-controlled Congress succeeds in constraining the president’s policy objectives on Ukraine, Trump may behave more chaotically on the world stage, not least because dealing with opposition is not his forte. Prevented from carrying out his domestic agenda, Trump may well seek to achieve his goals in the foreign policy sphere, where since 9/11 the executive has accumulated more power to pursue its aims, such as heading diplomacy efforts and military operations, with limited congressional involvement. Post-election, Trump has reminded voters of his veto authority, which Congress can only override with two-thirds majorities in both chambers, and which the Democrats do not have.

In its analysis of the U.S. midterms, the Kremlin-aligned Lenta.ru news site made a similar observation , with political analyst Georgii Asatrian predicting that a frustrated American president is more likely to focus on the international arena: “A paradox is possible: the president will try to compensate for his limitations within the country by increased foreign policy activity.’” Political scientist Anastasia Gafarova told Kremlin-aligned Gazeta.ru the same thing : “Given his severely weakened domestic political powers, it seems Trump will try to achieve historic successes precisely in that dimension which is institutionally more vested in the executive branch, namely, foreign policy.”

A far more defiant note was struck by the state-controlled media organization RT, which insisted that U.S. policy toward Ukraine and Russia is unlikely to change. Associate Professor at RUDN University Nikolai Parkhit’ko told RT : “It’s too early to talk about a landslide Democratic victory. […] The Democratic Party has sensible politicians who are discussing reducing aid [to Ukraine] which comes primarily from the pockets of American taxpayers. Kyiv is celebrating right now, as though Ukraine has flown to Venus and the rest of us are all left here to die. But it’s utterly immature and ill-conceived to think that tomorrow Zelensky will be given a trillion dollars, it’s shortsighted.” Although there are no Democrats who publicly discuss reducing Ukraine aid, this sally aligns with similar RT efforts that target U.S. voters as part of wider influence operations that weave populist grievances into pro-Russian narratives, in this case lamenting the loss of hard-earned American tax dollars in order to undermine public support for Ukraine.

The media assessments vary because they serve different purposes. If Russia is unable to achieve its objectives in Ukraine or make dialogue breakthroughs with Washington, it will be convenient to blame Democratic interference and military support for Kyiv. At the same time, the coverage reassures Russian readers that Trump ultimately has final say over U.S.-Russia relations, and even if he didn’t, Moscow’s decision-making does not rely on political shifts in Washington. After all, although Russia has often regarded Trump as useful, its most recent foreign policy concept has assessed that the United States seeks to weaken Russia and undermine its economic and technological capabilities while threatening its sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Finally, the repeated prophecy in pro-Russian news outlets of escalating tensions between the U.S. Congress and a president who, they insist, will be aggressively focused on making unilateral foreign policy decisions that undermine the Democratic agenda, is consistent with the Kremlin’s own preference for American disruption, distraction, and gridlock. The more disunited and dysfunctional the American government is, the less effective it will be in challenging Russian ambitions.
